## block 2 — where that gap could come from
One compaction sits inside the A..B segment. A compaction re-reads the whole
context to summarise it, and that call is not written to the transcript as an
assistant turn, so its tokens are outside this basis by construction.

417fef89 (Opus, open across both readings):
  compaction markers: 2
    2026-09-20T20:33:30.897Z  system  compact_boundary   <- inside A..B
    2026-09-20T20:33:29.833Z  user  isCompactSummary   <- inside A..B
  largest raw input_tokens on any one request: 2 — a full uncached context read would appear here as a large number
c5571add (the Sonnet run, inside A..B):
  compaction markers: 0
  largest raw input_tokens on any one request: 4 — a full uncached context read would appear here as a large number

marker lines inside A..B, across both sessions: 2
minutes from the located compaction to reading B: 1.8

What this shows is narrower than a mechanism: a compaction happened inside
the segment, and no request in either transcript carries an input large
enough to be a whole-context read. Whether Claude Code writes a
summarisation call to the transcript at all is not demonstrated here.

And the direction does NOT follow. An earlier version of this file argued
that a cost the basis cannot see can only be missing, never double-counted,
so the segment total was a FLOOR. Block 1 above refutes that in its own
first row: at reading A the transcript basis is +1.48% ABOVE Claude Code's
own figure. The same method overstates there. So the disagreement runs both
ways across the two observations that exist — +1.48% at A, -10.69% at B —
and the segment total is a figure with a two-sided uncertainty of roughly
that size, not a bound. Every per-point rate below inherits that.

## block 4 — what else on disk carries a rate limit
An earlier draft of the report claimed nothing but the statusline payload
holds anything about rate limits, and that transcripts do not. That is wrong,
and this block is what corrected it: a transcript can carry a `quotaLimits`
field. It holds no percentage, so it is no use as a series — but it records
the moment a request was REFUSED for hitting a cap, which a percentage never
does. Counted over every transcript on the machine, top level and subagents.

transcripts scanned (top level and every subagents tree): 4691
lines carrying a `quotaLimits` object: 13
fields it ever carries: isUsingOverage, lowPriorityMaxWaitSeconds, lowPriorityOffer, lowPriorityRetryAfterSeconds, overageDisabledReason, overageStatus, rateLimitType, resetsAt, status, unifiedRateLimitFallbackAvailable
a percentage among them? NO

session	at	rateLimitType	status	resetsAt

Each of these is a cap actually reached. That is a stronger anchor than a
rounded percentage — at the moment of a refusal the meter is at its limit, so
the window spend up to that instant is a denominator and not a band. Nothing
in this report uses it yet; it is the next measurement, not this one.
